passage:
I'm Imran, and I sit two desks from Jagdish, our junior auditor. On Tuesday I saw him frown at his screen for a long time. He'd noticed the same vendor being paid again and again, with nothing in the delivery register to match.

I expected him to blurt out a conclusion. Instead he murmured, half to himself, "Could be a filing gap. Could be another receiving log. What would tell error from wrongdoing? Delivery notes, a purchase order, an approval trail." He wrote three words on a sticky note and went to check the archive room.

I can't say what he was feeling. He looked calm, though he chewed his pen a lot. I just know he didn't call anybody a thief that day.

qa.q: Where did Jagdish go after writing on the sticky note?
qa.a: He went to check the archive room.

qa.q: What might Jagdish have been feeling as he chewed his pen while checking the vendor payments?
qa.a: He may have been uneasy or cautious, though Imran admits he only looked calm and cannot be sure.

qa.q: What else could Jagdish do if the archive room had no papers, and why?
qa.a: He could ask the receiving staff whether deliveries were logged somewhere else, because a missing record has innocent explanations too and each answer narrows the picture.

qa.q: How does Imran see Jagdish's caution compared with rushing to conclude?
qa.a: Imran expected a hasty accusation and instead saw restraint, which protects people who may turn out to be innocent.

grounding: An auditor notices repeated vendor payments without delivery records and reasons about alternative explanations before judging.

passage:
Monday. In her third month as a junior auditor, Shreya notices it in the ledger of a client's Pune plant: eleven invoices from the same packaging vendor, paid over six months, and no goods-received note for any of them. Her first thought is fraud. Her second is: slow down.
Tuesday. Over lunch she thinks aloud with Aadhya, a batchmate on another audit. 'What else could explain it? The notes could be filed in another system. The vendor could supply services, not goods. Or someone made a data-entry mistake that keeps repeating.' Aadhya asks, 'So what would tell you which one?' Shreya writes a list: check the other system, check the purchase orders, ask stores how deliveries are logged.
Thursday. The other system has nothing. The purchase orders describe cartons, not services. Stores has no record. Shreya writes up what she found and what she ruled out, and takes it to her audit senior before saying the word 'fraud' to anyone. The senior reads it twice. 'Good. We'll take this to the audit manager today.'

qa.q: How many invoices from the vendor did Shreya find?
qa.a: Eleven invoices from the same packaging vendor.

qa.q: What did Shreya feel at first, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: Alarm and suspicion of fraud, which she deliberately slowed down so her judgement would not run ahead of the facts.

qa.q: Why was it wise to list other explanations first?
qa.a: Checking whether the gap was a filing or data error meant any report would rest on evidence, not a guess.

qa.q: How might the audit senior see Shreya's write-up?
qa.a: As careful and fair, since it shows both what was found and what was ruled out, making it easy to take further.

grounding: Shows a junior auditor noticing payments with no delivery record and testing other explanations and evidence before concluding anything.

passage:
Varun, you rushed into my cabin saying 'fraud'. Sit. Let old Noor tell you about my second year as an auditor.
At a textile client in Surat, I found forty payments to one dyeing unit, and no delivery slips. I was so sure. I had the email half-written to my manager: 'Suspected fraud.' Then I stopped and asked myself: what else could explain this? A different filing system. A different department receiving the goods. A clerk entering the same thing wrongly again and again.
So I checked each one. I went to the dyeing department myself. The slips were there, in a steel cupboard, in a separate register nobody in accounts had ever seen. Every payment matched.
If I'd sent that email, I would have accused a clean team, and they would never have trusted an auditor again.
Sometimes it is fraud, Varun. When it is, the facts will still be there tomorrow. So. Tell me the other explanations first.

qa.q: Where were the delivery slips found?
qa.a: In a steel cupboard, in a separate register.

qa.q: How did young Noor feel before checking the other explanations?
qa.a: Very sure and eager to report it, with the email half-written, before choosing to slow down.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Noor's story, and what did it prevent?
qa.a: Stopping to list other explanations before sending the email; it prevented falsely accusing an honest team.

qa.q: How might the dyeing department team have felt if the email had been sent?
qa.a: Wrongly accused and hurt, and likely distrustful of auditors afterwards.

grounding: Shows an auditor who finds payments with no delivery slips asking what else could explain them and checking before concluding.
